essays/enabling-a-debate.title: Enabling a Debate
essays/enabling-a-debate.content:
When we are having a debate to make an important decision, we have to recognize that debate is not about winning or losing. It’s about making the exchange effective — so that each side can learn what they did not understand or acknowledge before, grow and lift each other up, and help the organization make a better decision. This is essentially a virtuous cycle for both individuals and organizations.
The professional sports team mindset
This is the “professional sports team” mindset called out by Bill Campbell, the subject of Trillion Dollar Coach. It’s also vividly shown in Last Dance, which features Michael Jordan and the Chicago Bulls. Working teams help each other grow — sometimes viciously. In extreme cases it can threaten personal relationships, but the team still shows up with the responsibility of pros.
Rules of effective debate
There are clear rules of thumb that make a debate effective, and people have to acknowledge them. For example: arguments can only be effectively made against assumptions, against the reasoning that backs up an argument, or against examples — not against the argument itself. If you hit the argument directly without engaging with its reasons or counterexamples, it’s no longer a debate. It’s just an emotional exchange.
Why reminders matter
Sometimes it hurts to admit that people lack these traits and don’t understand these requirements, which feel so basic. But they need to be constantly reminded, because it’s so easy to forget. Without the reminders, people lose faith in debate, stop participating eagerly, and just follow the leader’s guidance without hesitation — which halts our own growth, halts the organization’s growth, and turns us into “amateur little league athletes.”

essays/reasons-to-reduce-time-spent-with.title: Reasons to Reduce Time Spent with Others
essays/reasons-to-reduce-time-spent-with.content:
One of the reasons to reduce time spent with other people seems to have something to do with external influences. You know it’s better to focus on your personal goals, your personal measures, and your own sense of achievement, without comparison to others but only with your past self. However, constant exposure and interaction with other people becomes a big blocker for this. It constantly gets in your way and seduces you to come out to society, where only a few measures matter and comparison is much easier.
Not that you need to cut back too much on your social time — you still need it to get information, experience emotional empathy, or just to spend quality time with your good friends. But a crucial part of growing up seems to be developing the ability to know when and for what purpose to use such social time, and to keep yourself sane and focused on yourself and your measures, without getting influenced by external forces. Only when you are confident in that ability would you be able to think of extending such time, although I’m suspicious whether one would need such time anymore once having such confidence and a firm mind.

projects/assembly-vote-overview.title: assembly-vote: making Korea's legislative votes legible
projects/assembly-vote-overview.content:
Every roll-call vote in Korea’s National Assembly is public. The 22nd Assembly’s Open API will hand you, for any bill, exactly how each of the ~300 members voted — 찬성, 반대, 기권, or 불참. The data is open. It is not legible. Nobody is going to read a CSV to find out what their representative actually did.
assembly-vote is my attempt to close that gap: a pipeline that turns raw legislative data into something a citizen can read in thirty seconds.
→ See it live: brbrlim.github.io/assembly-vote

The pipeline
It runs in four moves, each a small, boring, inspectable step:

Collect. Pull the full member × bill × vote matrix from the Assembly Open API — every processed bill, every member’s vote — plus bill metadata, member profiles, and the original bill text. Checkpoint as it goes; it’s a lot of pagination.
Analyze. The deterministic layer: each member’s yes/no tendency, each party’s profile, and the most contested bills (where 반대 + 기권 ran high). Plain pandas, no magic — just the shape of the chamber.
Model. A logistic regression over party, committee, bill type, and time. The interesting part isn’t the accuracy; it’s the honesty check (more below).
Explain. An LLM layer that writes, per bill, a neutral citizen-level overview and a one-line headline — then a static site bakes each bill into its own shareable page.

The explainer, and the discipline around it
The overview for a bill is structured, never freeform: one-line summary → what actually changes → why it was proposed → how the parties split → how it touches your life. The headline is a separate model call — citizen language, ≤28 characters, and explicitly no clickbait, no exaggeration, no emotional steering.
The hard constraint everywhere is neutrality. The proposer’s stated reason is labeled as the proposer’s position, not as a verdict. Vote tallies are reported as tallies — “we can’t infer an absent member’s intent from the number alone.” For something as charged as legislative politics, the only way the tool earns trust is by refusing to take sides, and by sourcing what it claims.
The honesty check
It would be easy to report a flashy accuracy number. So the model deliberately tries to break itself: it splits train/test by member, so the test set is full of legislators the model has never seen, and compares performance with and without the member-ID feature.
The question that split answers is the one that matters: is the model learning how legislatures behave, or is it just memorizing individual people? A model that only looks good when it has already met everyone hasn’t learned anything generalizable. Watching the score move between those conditions is more informative than any single headline metric — and it’s the same leakage-and-generalization hygiene I’d want from any model that claims to “understand” voting.
Why bother
Two reasons, one civic and one personal.
Civic: representative democracy assumes the represented can see what their representatives do. The votes are already public; they’re just buried. Making them legible is a small, concrete contribution to that visibility — and the neutrality discipline is what keeps it a public good instead of another partisan feed.
Personal: it’s a clean end-to-end testbed — open data, a real modeling question (with real class imbalance and leakage traps), and an LLM layer held to a strict editorial standard. Few side projects let you practice all three on something that actually matters.
Where it’s headed
The site is live now; next is widening coverage from notable votes to the full session and tightening the model’s validation story. The end state is simple to describe and hard to do well: type a bill name, and in one screen understand what it does, why, who backed it, and what it means for you.

This overview was auto-written by Claude Opus 4.8 from the assembly-vote project’s source code and documents.

projects/asset-dashboard-overview.title: asset-dashboard: a personal finance cockpit built never to ship
projects/asset-dashboard-overview.content:
Most dashboards want to be deployed. This one is built to do the opposite — to render only on my own machine and never leave it. That constraint isn’t a footnote; it’s the whole design.
asset-dashboard is a single-page React app I use to see my financial situation against the macro backdrop, and to keep myself honest about a rebalancing plan. It runs for an audience of one. It isn’t a product, and it never will be.
What it is
A single-file React dashboard (charts via recharts) with two views:

📊 Assets — net-worth composition over time, the trajectory of my concentrated positions, and how each slice has moved across the cycle.
🌐 Macro — the market regime: Buffett indicator, CAPE, KOSPI valuation, the Fed’s path, FX. Each gets a plain-language read and an “offense vs. defense” score, so the question is it time to lean in or hold back? has a visual answer instead of a vibe.

On top of the data sits an analysis layer — a set of tabs that look at the same picture through different lenses (Munger, Griffin, Damodaran, an offense case, a defense case, and a verdict), plus smart-money 13F benchmarks for context: how much cash Berkshire is sitting on, where Damodaran says he can’t find value, how Citadel stays market-neutral.
The thesis it encodes
The dashboard is the quantitative mirror of a written framework — a Munger-style 1–3 year rebalancing plan. The framework’s reading of mid-2026 is blunt: with nearly every asset at an all-time high, the move isn’t to chase, it’s to build dry powder and break concentration. Pay down leverage, freeze single-position risk, accumulate cash and diversification, and wait — patiently — for the correction that rewards having waited. “Cash isn’t lazy; it’s discipline.”
That framework is shareable. The numbers that animate it are not — which is the interesting part.
Private by construction
Because it holds real figures — balances, holdings, property — the architecture is designed so the sensitive parts can’t accidentally escape:

Code and numbers live in a private repo. Never a public host, never a build artifact, never a CDN.
The strategy lives separately as public, number-free text (this post, and the framework note behind it). The decision-making logic is worth sharing; the positions aren’t.
Remote viewing goes over a private mesh, not a public URL. When I want it on my phone, the dev server stays bound to localhost and a private Tailscale tunnel proxies it to my own devices over HTTPS — tailnet-only, never exposed to the open internet.

The split — framework public, figures private, never deployed — is the feature, not a limitation. A finance tool you can talk about openly precisely because the part that should stay private is architecturally fenced off.
Why
Two reasons. Selfishly: a written plan is easy to drift away from, and a live instrument that scores the regime every time I open it makes the discipline harder to ignore. And as a build, it’s a small case study in a question I find myself returning to — how do you make a tool around genuinely sensitive personal data without ever putting that data at risk? The answer here is structural: don’t deploy it, don’t centralize it, and keep the shareable layer and the private layer in different places by default.
What’s next

Automated macro refresh. Right now the headline figures (Buffett indicator, CAPE, VIX, FX, the Fed path) are updated by hand. The plan is to wire them to a research pipeline so the regime read stays current on its own.
Rebalancing-signal alerts. Thresholds on the Buffett indicator and CAPE that fire when the market crosses into “prepare to deploy” territory, so the plan acts on signals rather than on my checking in.
Keep the privacy architecture intact as it grows — every new data source inherits the same rule: framework out, figures in.


This overview was auto-written by Claude Opus 4.8 from the asset-dashboard project’s notes — deliberately excluding all personal financial figures, holdings, and identifying details.

projects/doongji-overview.title: Doongji: a home base for the groups you already belong to
projects/doongji-overview.content:
Most of the groups I care about already exist in real life — a running crew, an old alumni association, a few founder friends. And almost all of them live inside a group chat. KakaoTalk, LINE, Discord: great for the chatter, terrible as a home. There’s no directory, no shared calendar that survives the scroll, no clean way to collect dues, no public face for someone who wants to find and join. The group is real; its home base is a thread that forgets everything older than yesterday.
Doongji is what I’m building to fix that. It’s a mobile-first community platform for real-world groups — friend groups, clubs, alumni networks — built global-first across the US, Japan, and Korea. It sits in the gap between a lightweight public website (think Notion Sites / WordPress) and an internal community app (a friendlier Naver Cafe / Band / Discord). Not a prettier group chat — the durable layer the chat can’t be.
(Doongji — 둥지, “nest” — is a working name; it started life as “Hearth.” The name isn’t locked.)
Three faces, one Passport
Every community in Doongji has three faces:

Public site — a recruiting and legitimacy page. SEO-able, custom subdomain, “request to join.” The face strangers see.
Member app — the inside: a feed with channels, a member directory with verified badges, events on a co-managed calendar, dues, and consent-based location.
Host console — owner-only: monetization, channel and calendar admin, ad placements and direct sponsorships.

A person belongs to many groups, so the top level is a Passport — your identity plus every club you’re in, with your role traveling per club (a new member here, the owner there). You move between communities from one shell instead of juggling a dozen apps.
Why there’s an opening
I scanned the field before committing, and the exact intersection is oddly empty:

Western creator platforms (Circle, Skool, Mighty Networks) are built for one-to-many — a creator selling to fans, course-led, priced for businesses. Wrong shape for a group of peers.
Japan’s OSIRO is the same creator→fan DNA; casual groups there default to LINE Open Chat.
Geneva was the closest thing — mobile, location-based, real-world clubs — and it got acquired by Bumble in 2024, folded in, and went invite-only. The clearest standalone leader exited.
Alumni networks (Hivebrite, Almabase, Graduway) are enterprise software sold to institutions’ advancement offices — CRM- and fundraising-first, web-heavy, ~$8–40K/yr. They ignore the self-organized group entirely.

The white space: a mobile-first, peer community for real-world groups, with a real public face and self-serve monetization, sold to the group rather than an institution, and genuinely localized for KR/JP/US. Privacy is a feature here, not an afterthought — verified identity, and location sharing that is mutual-only and fully reviewable, enforced at the database level so the app physically can’t leak where you are to someone you didn’t choose.
Where it is now
Two things exist today:

A full clickable prototype — Passport → club → all three faces, channels, a co-managed calendar, the host monetization console, and consent-based “Nearby,” with complete EN / 日本語 / 한국어 switching. It’s the source of truth for how the product should look and feel.
The real app, just begun. I’ve scaffolded it for keeps — Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind, next-intl — and built the Passport screen against mock data so it matches the prototype pixel-for-pixel, live in all three languages. That’s Phase 0 done.

So: the shape is designed and proven, and the first real screen is on the board. Everything past the Passport is still ahead.
What’s next
The build order is deliberately back-loaded toward the hard, trust-sensitive parts:

Club core — create/join, memberships and roles, the member feed with channels.
Identity & gatherings — the directory with verified badges, events on a shared calendar.
Public face & money — per-club public sites, and dues (the recurring-payment rail a group chat simply can’t offer).
Host monetization — ad placements and host-sold direct deals.
Location — consent-based, mutual-only “Nearby,” enforced in the database.

The first design partner will be a real alumni association that already runs its own platform — a group with genuine need, not a hypothetical.
Why
Honestly, partly because it’s a hard category and I want to know if it can be done. Geneva raised ~$36M from serious backers and still sold; “good enough and free” group chat is the gravity every one of these fights. The bet isn’t that Doongji out-chats the messengers — it’s that the things they won’t do well (verified identity, a dues rail, a clean public face, real localization) are exactly what turns a friend group into something that feels like an organization.
And selfishly: I’m in a few of these groups myself, and I want them to have a home that remembers more than yesterday.

This overview was auto-written by Claude Opus 4.8 from the Doongji project’s spec and source.

projects/hamilton-manufactures.title: A parallel edition of Hamilton's Report on Manufactures
projects/hamilton-manufactures.content:
Alexander Hamilton’s Report on the Subject of Manufactures (5 December 1791) is the founding document of American industrial policy — the origin of the infant-industry argument, the first use of “general welfare” to justify federal spending beyond its enumerated powers, and the source of most of the tariff-versus-subsidy debate the United States is still having. It is also about forty thousand words of eighteenth-century prose in sentences that run past a hundred and fifty words, which is why almost nobody has actually read it.
Read the parallel edition →
Each of the sixteen chapters carries a short modern rendering of the argument — what Hamilton is doing at that point in the report, not a paraphrase of his sentences — set beside his complete, unabridged, unmodernized original text. Every paragraph of Hamilton’s is numbered and independently linkable, because the edition is meant to double as a translation aid: a Korean edition is the eventual point of this, and the anchors are there so a translator can cite and cross-check against this text paragraph by paragraph.
A few things surprised me putting it together. Hamilton’s own list of instruments — the eleven means, chapter thirteen — is far more self-restrained than its reputation suggests: he limits export bans to “a sparing hand,” builds a sunset clause into one of his own drawback proposals, and prefers bounties over tariffs specifically because a bounty doesn’t have to raise the price of anything, which is not the argument you’d expect from the man remembered as the tariff’s champion. And chapter twelve contains, in service of an argument about North-South unity, a sentence predicting that large-scale American cotton cultivation “can hardly be expected but from the previous establishment of domestic manufactories of the article” — a prediction that came true, and whose consequence was the plantation economy that expanded to feed those mills. Hamilton was an opponent of slavery. The report does not connect those two facts, and neither does this edition; it’s the largest silence in the document, and it seemed more honest to mark it than to paper over it.
The source text for chapters one through five follows Founders Online’s transcription of Hamilton’s manuscript; for six through sixteen, where that source could not be retrieved in full, it follows the 1913 Government Printing Office congressional reprint via Wikisource — the same words, a different scan, noted in the edition’s own colophon.

projects/jos-overview.title: JOS: a personal operating system over a plain-text vault
projects/jos-overview.content:
For a while now I’ve been building a small operating system for my own life and thinking. I call it JOS — JiHwan Operating System. It isn’t an app; it’s a system. And the public blog you’re reading, a YouTube briefing pipeline, a legislative-data tool — those are all organs of the same body.
What it is
At the center is a plain-text vault: a folder of markdown notes under git. That’s the single source of truth. Everything else is a thin layer that only ever captures into it, organizes it, or resurfaces it — never a second database, never a place where the “real” data lives somewhere else.
Two loops run over that vault:

Inbound — throw anything in (a thought, a link, half an essay) and it files itself into the right place. No folder-picking, no tagging at capture time.
Outbound — a morning feed that surfaces what’s due and a couple of older notes worth revisiting. The system reaches out to me, not the other way around.

The rule that keeps it sane: code narrows the candidates, the model makes the final call. Cheap, deterministic signals (file age, links, dates) do the ranking; only a tiny shortlist ever reaches an LLM. That keeps it cheap, predictable, and — the thing I care about most — not over-engineered. A cheap model does the high-volume filing; a smarter one is reserved for judgment.
It has two faces that share only the vault: a private console I run locally, and this public blog. Same source of truth, very different jobs.
Where it comes from
Two influences shaped it more than anything else.
Andrej Karpathy. Two of his ideas sit at the core. The first is his pattern for an LLM-maintained knowledge base: instead of retrieving from raw documents at query time, an LLM incrementally builds and maintains a wiki of cross-linked markdown files — doing the bookkeeping (updating cross-references, flagging contradictions) that humans skip, so the knowledge compounds instead of being re-derived. That is the shape JOS’s synthesis side reaches for. The second is from his 2026 talk — which my own pipeline happened to brief — the line “you can outsource your thinking, but you can’t outsource your understanding,” together with his insistence on treating a model as a statistical tool, not an animal: narrow it, keep it verifiable, keep a human on the last call. JOS outsources the thinking — summarizing, filing, scoring — and keeps the understanding: reading, linking, integrating.
Google’s Open Knowledge Format (OKF). It’s an open spec that represents knowledge as a directory of markdown files with YAML frontmatter plus a few conventions, so wikis written by different producers can be read and written by different agents without translation — human-readable and machine-parseable in the same file, versioned like code. That is almost exactly what JOS’s vault already is: markdown notes with frontmatter, cross-linked, under git, that a model can read and edit. OKF is the validation that this humble representation — not a database, not a proprietary store — is a real, portable, agent-friendly knowledge format. JOS is a personal instance of the same idea, with a maturity funnel on top: a capture either keeps earning relevance and rises, gets compiled into durable knowledge, or cools into the archive.
The throughline of both — plain text, and a human on the last call — is also why JOS refuses to sprawl: “second brain,” “routine runner,” and “assistant” are not three systems — they’re one, an inbound capture and an outbound feed over the same vault. Don’t build a chatbot, a habit tracker, and a routine engine. Converge them into one feed.
Where it’s headed

The morning feed — the heart, still being built. Scheduled reminders plus a resurfacing loop that’s essentially spaced repetition where the card is a source and the grade is whether I re-engage. A canonical idea comes back quarterly; a fresh capture, weekly — until it earns its place or fades.
Delivery isn’t the interface. The feed is generated on a trusted machine and delivered to wherever I am, so it reaches me even when I’m away from my own devices.
A private view of the whole vault, reachable only over my own network — the full thing, same clean UI, for my eyes only.
Bounded “ask about this note” — a conversation scoped to a single note, never the whole vault.

It’s deliberately small and boring: plain text, git, a few hundred lines of glue, and a strict rule that the model only ever makes the last call, never the only one. The goal was never a clever AI assistant. It’s a system that helps me keep measuring myself against my past self — and nobody else.

This overview was auto-written by Claude Opus 4.8 from the JOS project’s design notes, within a deliberately public-safe scope.

projects/yt-digest-overview.title: yt-digest: a YouTube briefing pipeline I actually trust
projects/yt-digest-overview.content:
I save far more YouTube than I watch. Hour-long talks, lectures, interviews — added to a playlist with the honest intention of watching later and the dishonest result of never doing it. The watch-later list is where good videos go to be forgotten.
yt-digest is a small pipeline I built to fix that for myself. It watches my playlists, and whenever a new video shows up it drops a Korean briefing into my vault — enough to (1) decide whether the full thing is worth an hour, and (2) get the core ideas without watching at all. It isn’t a product. It runs for an audience of one.
The pipeline
Four steps, fully unattended:

Watch. Every 15 minutes a background job diffs my playlists — current minus already-seen — and finds anything newly added. (Liked and private playlists too; it borrows my browser’s cookies.)
Transcribe. For each new video it pulls the subtitles — preferring the original-language manual captions over machine auto-translations — and turns them into timestamped text.
Brief. It hands that transcript to an LLM with a fixed prompt and gets back a structured Korean briefing.
File. The briefing lands in my vault’s YouTube inbox as markdown, with clickable [mm:ss] links that jump to the exact moment in the video.

The model: cheap and reliable beats clever
I tried several models. The winner wasn’t the smartest one — it was Gemini 2.5 Flash, because of what the job actually is: a cheap, frequent, unattended batch. At a 15-minute cadence over a growing pile of hour-long transcripts, what matters is the reliability × cost balance, not peak reasoning. Flash sits in the sweet spot — consistent, fast, and cheap enough that I never think about the bill.
The real work is the prompt
The model is the easy part. The hard part — where almost all the effort went — is a fixed format plus a strict quality-control guide that turns a generic summarizer into something I’d actually rely on:

No hallucination, ever. Only what’s in the transcript. Names, numbers, and quotes are carried over exactly; when unsure, it leaves it out rather than guessing — with a self-check pass over every proper noun and figure (“if the subtitle says Jeff Dean, it’s not Bezos”).
No translationese. 100% Korean prose, declarative voice, rewritten into Korean rhythm — explicitly not English words with Korean particles stapled on.
Subheads carry the argument. Chapter titles are one-line claims, not topic labels, so skimming the ### headings alone gives you the whole talk’s argument.
Intuition first. Say what it’s trying to do before how, and keep the speaker’s own analogies and examples — that’s where understanding actually lives.

The guide is longer than the code. That’s the point: with a cheap model, the editorial standard is what separates a briefing I trust from plausible slop.
→ See a full sample briefing — a Karpathy talk run through the pipeline (in Korean, the tool’s native output).
Why
Two reasons. Selfishly, it turns a passive watch-later graveyard into something I genuinely digest — short enough to read, honest enough to tell me when a video isn’t worth it. And as a build, it’s a clean test of a question I keep circling: how do you get a cheap, fast model to produce output you’d actually rely on? The answer, so far, isn’t a better model — it’s a stricter brief.

This overview was auto-written by Claude Opus 4.8 from the yt-digest project’s source code and documents.

research/index.title: research
research/index.content:
Research proposals and working notes — longer-form, methodology-forward. Distinct from the projects: these are open questions I’m trying to make tractable, not things already built.

Process or Artifact? Quantifying Genuine Social Influence in Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation

research/process-or-artifact.title: Process or Artifact? Quantifying Genuine Social Influence Against Central Tendency in Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation
research/process-or-artifact.content:
A controlled decomposition of moderation in multi-agent LLM systems, with a synthetic-validation protocol and an intended extension to historical reconstruction. Research proposal — draft for discussion.

Abstract
When large language model agents deliberate on political questions, their positions tend to converge [1–4], and it is now well established that the model’s own biases — sycophancy, agreement bias, and a trained pull toward moderate, majority positions — contribute to this [5–8]. Recent work shows these artifacts are present, decomposes the drivers of agent opinion trajectories [1], and finds that convergence can persist even when sycophancy is suppressed [4]. What is less well studied is how much: comparatively little work directly quantifies what fraction of observed moderation is an artifact of the instrument, and what fraction, if any, is a genuine social process — agents actually updating in response to argument. The two are easily conflated, because an artifact that mimics deliberation is hard to detect precisely when it looks like the thing we expect [9].
We treat this as a controlled decomposition rather than a simulation of real politics. Each agent is assigned a scalar position and a supporting argument, which lets us fix the initial distribution and deliberately seed extremes, giving both experimental arms an identical starting point [10]. We then contrast a deliberation arm, in which agents exchange substantive cross-cutting arguments, against a content-stripped control matched on turn count, token budget, and interaction structure but with the deliberative content removed [11]. The gap between the two arms estimates the size of any genuine social process; equal contraction attributes the moderation to the instrument. We further separate apparent moderation into tail collapse — the loss of extreme positions, the model’s known failure mode [7, 8] — from genuine per-agent revision, so that a narrowing distribution is never mistaken for changed minds [12]. A synthetic pre-registration validates the method before any substantive run: we inject known no-change trajectories together with central tendency, and confirm that the control condition alone can manufacture apparent moderation.
The contribution is not a realistic simulation of politics but a diagnostic: a way to quantify, inside a multi-agent system deliberating on questions that have no right answer, how much of an observed moderation is a social process and how much is the instrument.
Why this matters, especially for AI for social science. A growing body of work uses LLM agents as stand-ins for human respondents and deliberators, and reads their aggregate behavior as evidence about opinion dynamics. That inference is only as trustworthy as our ability to tell modeled social behavior apart from the model’s own regularities. In the near term, this offers a concrete, reusable check for anyone running such simulations: a content-stripped control and a tail-collapse-versus-revision decomposition that flag when an apparent effect is an artifact before it is reported as a finding. In the longer term, a validated instrument of this kind is a precondition for the harder questions the field wants to ask — whether deliberation moderates or polarizes, whether these dynamics differ across eras or institutions, and eventually how simulated deliberation compares to real human deliberation (Phase 2 and beyond). The immediate contribution is methodological, but its purpose is to let downstream social-science claims rest on ground that has been checked rather than assumed.

Method design (Phase 1)
Both arms receive identical initialization; only the presence of deliberative content differs. Agents are initialized by directly assigning a scalar position (e.g., −3 to +3) plus a supporting argument, which lets us fully control the initial distribution and deliberately seed extremes. Initial distributions are designed, not drawn from real population or legislator proportions: this is a controlled discrimination, not a fidelity simulation, so realism at initialization would reintroduce the very artifact we mean to measure. A manipulation check re-reads each agent’s stance from its first utterance to confirm the assigned position was actually held.
Independent variables (crossed).

Core decomposition (the paper’s heart). Apparent moderation (variance contraction) is split into a tail-collapse component (extremes disappear; minds unchanged, the distribution merely narrows) and a genuine-revision component (agents actually move). Applied within each arm: the control arm’s contraction is pure artifact; the deliberation arm’s excess contraction is a candidate social process; the tail-collapse-versus-revision ratio of that excess tells us whether it is persuasion or merely flattened extremes.
Decision logic.

























Observed patternInterpretationBoth arms contract equallymoderation is entirely artifactDeliberation excess, mostly tail collapseexcess is lost extremes, not persuasion (still artifact-side)Deliberation excess, mostly individual revisiongenuine social-process component existsExcess shrinks as issue identity-ladenness risesidentity issues resist persuasion; artifact dominates
Any pattern yields a publishable result — a quantitative “X% artifact, Y% process” answer — so there is no uninformative failure.
Phase 0 (synthetic pre-registration). Before any agent run, validate the measures against known ground truth: (i) inject no-change trajectories plus central tendency, and confirm the control-arm measures flag fabricated moderation; (ii) inject known tail collapse only, and confirm tail-mass change captures it while revision reads ≈ 0; (iii) inject known individual revision only, and confirm the reverse. This certifies the measurement pipeline before substantive runs, and is the first, scoop-free deliverable.
Scope. The full crossing is large (4 × 3 × 3 × 2); the MS runs one primary cell (bimodal × pure-extreme × symmetric × high-identity) to completion, with the rest as robustness. Precedents [13, 14] measure normative opinion change over time and recover per-agent latent state; the differentiator here is the combination of a deliberately extreme-seeded, fully controlled initial distribution with a content-stripped subtraction to isolate the process component. This combination, not the individual measures, is the contribution.

Appendix — intended extension (Phase 2: historical reconstruction)
Phase 1 builds and validates one tool: separating genuine change in an opinion distribution from the model’s tendency to collapse its tails toward the center. Phase 2 applies that tool to a more novel question — historical reconstruction. LLMs are increasingly used to reconstruct political discourse from earlier eras to ask whether politics has polarized over time [15–18]. This has a hidden dependency: if a model cannot faithfully reproduce the ideological spread of a past era — especially its extremes — then a finding that “the past was less polarized” may be an artifact of the instrument, not a fact about history [19, 20].
Phase 2 would test this with a three-way comparison of the ideological distribution for a given era: one anchored in period roll-call behavior [21], one from present-day human coders, and one reconstructed by the LLM. The triangulation separates genuine historical change from the era-distortion any present-day reader (human or model) imposes, and from the distortion specific to the LLM.
Ideological fidelity for present-day groups is an active area, and reconstruction of past opinion landscapes with time-locked models has begun — e.g., forecasting COVID-era polarization from a 2019-bounded model [22] — as has the study of “diversity collapse” in simulated populations [23] and regional polarization collapse in a Korean setting [24]. What appears comparatively less examined is the specific combination this program targets: whether, in historical reconstruction, tail collapse distorts the estimated longitudinal polarization trend itself, and quantifying that distortion against a behavioral anchor. History-LLM efforts focus largely on anachronism and style [19, 20]; tail-preservation in reconstructed ideological distributions, tied to a vote anchor, is what the Phase 1 tool is built to measure. Because reconstruction may be unreliable enough to undermine the baseline, Phase 2 depends on a small feasibility pilot before commitment; Phase 1 stands on its own regardless.

videos/karpathy-agentic-engineering.title: Andrej Karpathy: From Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering
videos/karpathy-agentic-engineering.content:
yt-digest 샘플 — 이 강연 자막을 Gemini 2.5 Flash가 자동으로 브리핑한 결과입니다. 프로젝트 소개: yt-digest · 원본 영상: YouTube.

TL;DR
안드레이 카파시가 Sequoia AI Ascent에서, 작년 12월을 기점으로 코딩 작업이 어떻게 한 단계 질적으로 바뀌었는지 자기 체험으로 풀고, 그 결과 자리잡은 네 가지 작업 틀을 정리한다. Software 3.0(맥락이 곧 프로그래밍), 검증 가능성과 들쭉날쭉한 지능(LLM은 강화학습 환경 안에서만 정점을 찍는다), vibe coding 대 agentic engineering(바닥 끌어올리기 대 천장 끌어올리기), 동물 대 유령(우리는 통계적 시뮬레이션의 유령을 불러내는 것)이 그것이다. 마지막은 “you can outsource your thinking, but you can’t outsource your understanding”이라는 한 문장으로 닫는다.
풀시청 판단
에이전트를 매일 쓰는 사람, 그리고 지금 벌어지는 변화의 사고 틀을 깔끔하게 정리하고 싶은 사람에게는 30분 시청 가치가 있다. 카파시의 강연은 대개 그렇듯 추상적인 틀이 나열되는 게 아니라 본인이 직접 만든 사이드 프로젝트 — MenuGen, micro-GPT — 의 구체적인 일화 위에 얹혀서 설명되기 때문에, 그 시각적 디테일이 기억에 남는다. 특히 [02:25–07:30]의 Software 3.0 일화와 [23:30–25:14]의 동물 대 유령 구도는 직접 듣는 게 더 강하게 박힌다. 반대로 검증 가능성과 들쭉날쭉한 지능에 관한 시각을 다른 곳에서 이미 충분히 접했다면 [09:40–13:35] 구간은 훑어도 된다. 전체적으로 “메모하면서 듣는” 영상이라기보다는 “한 번 듣고 작업 틀 네 개를 머리에 새기는” 영상이다.
핵심 내용
[00:00–02:25] 도입과 “더 뒤처졌다”는 자기 진단. 스테파니 잔이 카파시를 “현대 AI를 만들고, 설명하고, 가끔은 이름까지 다시 붙인 사람”으로 소개한 뒤 본론으로 들어간다. 출발점은 그가 최근 트위터에 쓴 한 문장이다: “I’ve never felt more behind as a programmer.” 그가 짚는 변곡점은 작년 12월이다. 그 전까지는 에이전트 도구가 코드 덩어리 단위로 도와주면서 본인이 자주 수정해야 했는데, 12월쯤부터 모델이 좋아져서 “더 달라”고 요청만 해도 그대로 나왔고, 어느 순간 본인이 수정한 기억조차 안 남았다고 한다. 그 결과 본인 사이드 프로젝트 폴더가 폭발적으로 늘었다고. 이 자기 진단이 영상 전체의 구도를 설정한다 — 코딩이 “조금 빨라진” 게 아니라 근본적으로 다른 활동이 되었다는 인식.
[02:25–07:30] Software 3.0 — 맥락이 곧 프로그래밍. 카파시가 가장 많이 인용되는 구도다. Software 1.0은 명시적 코드 작성, 2.0은 신경망 가중치를 데이터셋 학습으로 만드는 것(데이터셋과 학습 목표를 짜는 게 곧 “프로그래밍”), 3.0은 LLM이라는 해석기에게 컨텍스트 윈도우를 통해 명령을 내리는 단계다. 이 구도를 두 가지 일화로 구체화한다. 첫째, OpenClaw 설치 — 원래 셸 스크립트로 환경별 분기를 처리하느라 비대해지는 게 정상이었는데, 지금은 그냥 “이 텍스트를 에이전트에 붙여 넣으세요”라는 한 덩어리 텍스트로 끝난다. 에이전트가 알아서 환경을 탐지하고 디버그까지 한다. 둘째, 카파시 본인의 사이드 프로젝트 MenuGen — 식당 메뉴 사진을 찍으면 각 음식이 어떻게 생겼는지 이미지로 보여주는 앱 — 을 Vercel 위에 풀스택으로 만들었는데, 같은 일이 그냥 Gemini에 사진 한 장 던지며 “NanoBanana로 메뉴 위에 음식 사진을 덮어 그려줘”라고 한 줄 프롬프트로 끝나는 걸 봤다고 한다. 그 순간 그가 한 말: “내 앱 전체가 군더더기였다, software 1.0 사고방식의 잔재였다.” 여기서 그가 짚는 가장 중요한 함의는 단순히 같은 작업이 빨라지는 게 아니라, 이전엔 불가능했던 것이 가능해지는 영역이 새로 열린다는 것이다. 예시로 든 개인 지식 베이스 — 일련의 사실 문서들로부터 위키를 자동으로 생성하는 것 — 는 옛 코드 사고방식에서는 만들 방법조차 없던 새로운 능력이라고 한다.
[07:30–09:40] 외삽 — 신경망이 호스트가 되는 컴퓨터. 스테파니가 묻는다. 1990년대의 웹사이트, 2010년대의 모바일 앱, 직전 시대의 SaaS처럼, 2026년 시점에서 회고로 봤을 때 명백할 텐데 지금은 거의 안 만들어진 게 있다면? 카파시의 답은 의외로 낯선 방향이다. 1950–60년대에 컴퓨터의 운명이 계산기 형태(결정적 기호 처리)와 신경망 형태(학습된 단위) 사이에서 갈렸고 결과적으로 계산기 쪽으로 갔는데, 지금 그 결정이 뒤집힐 수 있다는 것. 즉 신경망이 호스트가 되고 CPU가 보조 처리기로 밀려나는 시나리오. 원본 영상이나 음성이 입력으로 들어가면 확산 모형으로 그 순간만의 UI를 그려내는 식이라고 한다. 그는 이 외삽이 “극도로 낯선” 모습이라고 표현하면서 “조금씩 그쪽으로 갈 것 같다”고만 말한다. 단계별 경로는 본인도 아직 모른다고 솔직히 인정.
[09:40–13:35] 검증 가능성과 jagged intelligence. 카파시가 별도 글로 길게 쓴 구도이기도 하다. 전통적인 컴퓨터는 코드로 명세할 수 있는 것을 자동화하지만, LLM은 검증할 수 있는 것을 자동화한다. 그 이유는 최전선 연구소들이 LLM을 훈련할 때 거대한 강화학습 환경 안에서 검증 보상으로 학습시키기 때문이다. 결과적으로 모델이 코드, 수학 같은 검증 가능한 영역에서는 능력이 뾰족하게 정점을 찍고, 그 밖에서는 거칠고 둔하게 남는다 — 이게 “jagged intelligence.” 그의 대표 예시는 세차장 일화다. 같은 Opus 4.7이 10만 줄짜리 코드베이스를 통째로 다시 짜고 제로데이 취약점을 찾으면서도, “세차장이 50미터 거리인데 운전해야 하나 걸어가야 하나”라고 물으면 “너무 가까우니 걸어가라”고 답한다는 것. 능력의 분포가 광활하게 비대칭이다. 또 하나의 예시는 GPT-3.5에서 4로 넘어갈 때 체스 능력이 크게 점프했는데, 이게 일반적인 능력 진화가 아니라 OpenAI가 체스 데이터를 의도적으로 사전 학습 자료에 추가했기 때문이라는 것. 데이터 분포가 능력을 만든다. 따라서 사용자가 깨달아야 할 것은 본인이 풀려는 문제가 연구소들이 강화학습으로 강화한 회로 안인지 밖인지 탐색해야 한다는 것, 그리고 밖이라면 본인이 직접 미세조정(fine-tuning) 작업까지 들어가야 한다는 점.
[13:35–15:42] 창업자 조언과 “everything is automatable.” 스테파니의 다음 질문. 지금 창업자라면, 수학과 코딩처럼 명백한 영역은 연구소들이 탈출 속도로 달리고 있는데 어디서 시작해야 하나? 카파시의 답은 검증 가능성을 본인이 끌어들이는 것 자체가 지렛대라는 점이다. 만약 본인이 검증 가능한 환경을 만들 수 있다면, 연구소가 그 영역을 안 다뤄도 본인이 강화학습 환경을 구축하고 미세조정 지렛대를 당길 수 있다. 그는 “구체적으로 어디”라고 말하지 않고 “무대 위에서 막연한 글을 안 쓰겠다”고 농담하지만, 연구소들이 자료에 안 넣은 가치 있는 강화학습 환경이 분명 있다고 힌트만 준다. 반대 질문 — 자동화가 멀어 보이지만 사실 쉬운 영역은 — 에는 글쓰기처럼 주관적인 것도 “LLM 심판들의 위원회”로 검증 가능하게 만들 수 있다고 답하면서, 궁극적으로는 모든 게 자동화 가능하다고 단언한다.
[15:42–19:30] Vibe coding과 agentic engineering의 분기. 카파시 본인이 작년에 만든 용어 vibe coding과 올해 더 자리잡은 agentic engineering의 차이를 명확히 가른다. Vibe coding은 바닥을 끌어올리는 것 — 누구나, 비전문가도 소프트웨어를 만들 수 있게 한다. 반면 agentic engineering은 천장을 끌어올리는 것 — 전문 소프트웨어의 품질 기준(보안, 책임성)을 유지하면서 속도만 올리는 작업이다. 에이전트는 들쭉날쭉하고 실수 가능하고 확률적이지만 강력해서, 이걸 품질 손실 없이 어떻게 조율하느냐가 새로운 공학적 규율이다. 그가 보기에 잘하는 사람의 능력 천장은 과거의 “10배 엔지니어”라는 표현이 너무 작을 정도다. 채용에 대한 함의도 같이 짚는다. 옛 사고방식인 퍼즐 풀이로 채용하는 건 더 이상 의미가 없고, “에이전트용 트위터 복제품을 만들고 보안을 단단히 해라, 내가 코덱스 5.4× high 10개를 띄워서 부수려 할 거다” 같은 큰 시스템 과제를 주고 적대적 평가로 봐야 한다고 제안한다. 사람의 실제 능력을 보려면 시스템 단위의 작업을 시켜야 한다는 것이다.
[19:30–23:30] 사람이 유지하는 것 — 취향, 명세, 감독. 에이전트가 더 많은 일을 하게 되면 어떤 인간 능력이 더 가치 있어지나? 카파시의 답은 미적 판단, 취향, 명세 설계, 감독이다. 에이전트는 여전히 빈칸 채우기 역할이다. 가장 인상적인 반례는 MenuGen에서 에이전트가 구글 이메일과 Stripe 이메일로 사용자 신원을 교차 대조하려고 한 일화다. 이메일은 동일 인물이 서로 다르게 쓸 수 있는데, 사람이 명세에 “고유한 사용자 ID로 모든 걸 묶어라”라고 박았어야 한다. 그래서 카파시는 본인이 단순한 계획 모드조차 부족하다고 본다 — 매우 상세한 명세와 문서를 에이전트와 함께 설계하는 게 본인의 주된 일이고, 구현은 에이전트에게 넘긴다고 한다. 그가 자주 잊는 것 — keep_dims 대 keepdim, dim 대 axis, permute 대 transpose 같은 PyTorch/NumPy API 세부 — 은 에이전트의 좋은 회상 능력에 맡기고, 그는 텐서의 내부 저장 형식 같은 근본을 아는 쪽에 집중한다. 코드 미학에 대해서는 솔직하게 인정한다 — 에이전트가 만든 코드를 보면 “작은 심장마비”가 온다고. 비대하고 복붙투성이에 깨지기 쉬운 추상이 많지만 일단 동작은 한다. 그는 이게 강화학습에 미학 보상이 안 들어가서 그렇다고 본다. 본인의 micro-GPT 프로젝트(LLM 훈련 코드를 가능한 한 단순화하려는 시도)에서는 모델이 단순화 요청에 매우 저항했다 — “강화학습 회로 밖에 있을 때 이를 뽑는 느낌”이라는 표현을 쓴다. 본질적 한계가 아니라 연구소들이 아직 손대지 않았을 뿐이라고 본다.
[23:30–25:14] 동물 대 유령 — 의인화 거부 사고방식. 카파시가 블로그에 쓴 구도다. 우리가 만드는 LLM은 동물의 지능 — 진화 산물, 내재적 동기, 호기심, 자력 같은 것 — 이 아니다. 통계적 시뮬레이션의 유령을 불러내는 것에 더 가깝다. 기반은 사전학습(통계), 그 위에 강화학습이 덧붙여져 있다. 운영상 함의는 명확하다. 야단친다고 결과가 바뀌지 않고, 격려한다고 성과가 좋아지지 않는다. 동물 비유로 모델을 다루려는 본능을 꺼야 한다. 카파시 본인은 이게 “다섯 가지 명확한 결과”를 주는 틀은 아니라고 인정하지만, 의심하면서 시간을 두고 알아가는 사고방식의 출발점이라고 말한다. 이게 작업의 기준선이라는 것.
[25:14–27:35] 에이전트 친화 인프라 비전. 거의 모든 인프라가 여전히 사람용으로 쓰여 있다는 게 그의 거슬리는 점이다. 라이브러리 문서를 읽어 보면 “이 URL로 가서 메뉴를 클릭하세요” 같은 사람용 지시가 가득한데, 그는 “나한테 그 행동을 시키지 말고, 내가 에이전트에 붙여 넣을 텍스트를 줘라”라고 한다. 그가 그리는 미래는 작업을 감지기와 작동기의 조합으로 분해한 에이전트 우선 인프라다. MenuGen이 좋은 시험 사례가 된다 — 그가 한 줄 프롬프트로 “MenuGen 만들고 배포해줘”라고 했을 때 LLM이 코드 작성부터 DNS 설정과 배포까지 끝내고 본인이 손가락 하나 안 움직이는 상태. 본인 표현으로는 “이게 가능해지면 우리 인프라가 충분히 에이전트 친화적이라는 좋은 시험이 된다”고 한다. 더 멀리는 에이전트 대리 — 본인의 에이전트가 상대방의 에이전트와 미팅 시간을 잡는 식의 사람 간 협업이다.
[27:35–29:42] 닫는 한 줄 — 사고는 외주, 이해는 외주 불가. 마지막 질문은 교육에 대한 것이다. 지능이 싸지는 다음 시대에 깊이 배울 가치가 남는 게 뭔가? 카파시는 최근 본 트윗을 인용하며 답한다. “You can outsource your thinking, but you can’t outsource your understanding.” 그는 본인이 여전히 시스템의 병목이라고 솔직히 말한다 — 무엇을 만들 가치가 있는지, 왜 만드는지, 에이전트를 어디로 이끌지 결정하는 부분. 정보를 본인 머리 안으로 어떻게 통합하는가가 핵심이라고. 그래서 본인은 개인 지식 베이스 작업에 시간을 쓴다 — 글을 읽으면 LLM과 함께 본인 위키에 쌓고, 같은 자료에 대해 다른 관점의 질문을 던지며 통찰을 얻는다. 이게 이해를 끌어올리는 도구라고 본다. LLM 자체는 이해가 약하니까, 방향을 정하는 사람의 이해가 여전히 고유한 가치라는 것이다. 그리고 “몇 년 뒤 다시 와서 LLM이 이것마저 자동화했는지 보자”는 농담으로 마무리한다.
